newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall in profit-taking, bonds weaker.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall in profit-taking, bonds weaker.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed weaker Tuesday after rebounding from a big sell-off as investors took profits after the market's record-breaking rally.
Bonds also weakened amid a spate of new corporate offerings.
The dollar was mixed after Britain's budget boosted the British pound and an announcement of big losses at Switzerland's largest bank lifted the dollar against the Swiss franc.
The 30-stock Dow Jones industrial average fell 19.38 points to 6,528.41, one day after climbing through 6,500 for the first time and setting its 11th record in the last 12 sessions.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,351 to 1,134 on heavy volume of 527 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index eked out a gain of 0.83 point to close at a record 1,281.20.

The market was taken on a roller coaster ride from the opening, as waves of computer programme trades sent the Dow spiralling higher, but then at its peak, knocked a full 70 points off the index, triggering New York Stock Exchange curbs as the losses exceeded 50 points.
"You've got to expect a little bit more of a roller coaster and a dicier tape with the market this extended," said Gregory Nie, technical analyst at Everen Securities in Chicago.
He said the bullish trend still seemed to be in place.
"There are a lot of sceptics still out there, and maybe they had some influence on tape action today," he said. "But I would hesitate to call this a reversal, the charts look good."
Gary Anderson of Anderson & Loe Inc., which advises money managers, said the blue-chip stocks were hit by profit-taking.
"The market zigs and zags some, but we are in a powerful uptrend," he said. "This bull market has gored a lot of pundits who thought it was dead and went bearish. It ain't dead yet."

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell a quarter point, or $2.50 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.45 percent from 6.43 percent at Monday's close. The yield and the price move in opposite directions.
The British pound rose to $1.6750 before slipping back to $1.6717 late Tuesday, up from $1.6683 late Monday.
After flirting with 1.53 German marks, the dollar slipped back to 1.5244 marks late in the session, a touch higher than 1.5236 marks late Monday. It dipped to 112.50 Japanese yen from 112.63 yen.

The dollar hit a 21-month high of 1.2964 Swiss francs on a report that Union Bank of Switzerland would take a $2.3 billion charge to cover expected bad loans as a result of weak Swiss economic growth. The dollar fetched 1.2905 Swiss francs in late trading, up from 1.2885 late Monday.
The price of gold steadied as Wall Street's jitters over the stock market helped lift the precious metal from its lowest level in 20 months.

On New York's Commodity Exchange, December gold closed up 0.20 cent at $374.70 an ounce, rebounding from $373.20, which was its lowest level since March 3, 1995. It was also the first higher close after four straight sessions of losses.
Comex copper for December delivery closed up 2.30 cents at 108.20 cents per pound after peaking at 109.90 cents -- the highest level since mid-June.
Natural gas prices sped higher as a second storm system was forming in the southern United States that might spread snow and frigid cold from Texas to the eastern seaboard.

Nymex January natural gas futures were up 8.7 cents at $3.581 per million British thermal units, off from the contract high of $3.68 set Friday. The $3.68 was the second highest price since December 1995, trailing only the volatile close Thursday when the expiring December contract hit $4.05.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 rose to an intraday record of 4,094.4 before closing just 13.8 points higher at 4,068.4 -- below its record close of 4,073.1 set Oct. 21. In Tokyo, the session, the Nikkei 225 was up 124.68 points at 21,418.25.
